item.content:encoded:
Can't I just be lazy? :|
Responses

He glanced at the testing chamber from within the observation room. The photobooth sat inside, as innocent as could be. A waiting D-class stood in front of it.

Your sentences are all "X did Y", not to mention the last two are fairly short and feel choppy. They don't flow together, in other words.

“Please enter SCP-715 and take a photo, D-129012,” Louef instructed.

Don't eschew "said".

D-129012 strolled in. “Hey, guys, this thing is busted,” the voice came from inside. “I’m trying to use it, but it’s not giving me any photos.”

Again, short sentences with basically the same structure, feeling choppy. That dialogue tag is slightly irregular; why not say his voice, or why not make him actually say it, instead of his voice saying it?

The somewhat confused looking D-129012 left the booth, and was stopped in front of the SCP object.

There's a lot of this, too, "the adverb adjective noun" phrases. That's a really short-hand way to impart information, and it doesn't really draw the reader in. Same goes for "his clone" later on.

That's basically all the error types, just continued on again and again throughout that first scene. I did also have an issue with

The test subject’s head snapped backwards in a shower of gore.

That's just a little over the top, same with the clone screaming a scream of "misery and terror" later on.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
In terms of sample size, I felt like it would be more impractical for the Foundation to waste a few hundred D-class for testing a Safe-class skip, which is why I kept it down. I originally had more tests than that, but people felt like it was tossing away too many D's, so I cut it down, even if it's not technically scientifically sound.

The spoon thing is a little silly, I admit.

The Moral Ambiguity Disorder is similar, but not entirely the same as PTSD. In this mindset, MAD more commonly describes a sense of cognitive dissonance, where the person knows what they're doing is wrong, but at the same time is right, due to the argument of "the greater good." Now, of course, not everyone likes utilitarianism, so of course, some people are very traumatized by that kind of thing. It's my own little spin of a disorder that I thought that I'd flesh out for the story.

Finally, what I was implying (and that people in chat seemed to get) was that Louef is far from healed of his problems. He's dealing with them, yes, but he's not over them by a long shot. Social events and games can help take his mind off of the crippling morality attack within him, but it's never going to fully cure his condition, because like most mental disorders, there is no real cure. The ending is somewhat bittersweet in that he's examining his issues, but realizing that he needs to move on and focus on other matters as well.

EDIT: This is supposed to be a reply to Kalinin

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
In terms of the article's logistics, a lot of what's going on feels silly. If the experiment with the photo booth was to simply find out whether killing the original had any effect, there surely was a better way involving less risk to everyone involved than just having a guard immediately blowing the D-Class subject's head off immediately. If the intent was "hmmm, what's going to happen if we kill a person that happens to look exactly like the test subject, will they be agitated and scared", don't hang out by the phone waiting for that Nobel, doctors.

And the thing with the spoon. So they wait for the spoon to snap the person's spine, and then immediately afterward the doctor's all like "tell me how you feel about that". C'mon. Also, I have to note that if the reason we're seemingly killing people for no reason is "sample size", you're going to need a hell of a lot more than 10 people to establish that. I would imagine that the Foundation has other methods of testing, or tries to find out other things about items like this, since I can't imagine the Foundation is killing thousands of people a week in the name of testing Safe class objects.

I'm also not certain about the whole "Moral Ambiguity Disorder" thing. It seems like what would be happening is a whole lot of researchers with PTSD on the site; I don't know that the Foundation needed to invent a brand-new disorder to explain people being traumatized. And then of course it's all fixable with game nights and Christmas parties. You spend the first part of the article repeatedly telling us how awful and horrible the things the doctor is doing, and the payoff doesn't seem to recognize the supposed enormity of cruelty involved in the experimentation at all.

item.title: Author Overview
item.content:encoded:
This tale actually arose from this discussion on the forums that got me thinking about how exactly the Foundation handles events like this.

Now, the reason why this contains two relatively under-appreciated SCP's is because it was originally written for the UAC, but I decided not to post this for the contest, seeing as the main topic in this tale isn't the SCP's themselves, but rather, their effect on the researcher.

Thanks to all of chat for reading this, and also their many attempts to name this piece.

Also, if you know where these guys are from, bonus points to you.
